title: Growing Old in Academe
author: Jonathan Imber
summary: Jonathan Imber, who has taught at Wellesley College for nearly four decades, offers a reflective essay on aging, retirement, and institutional memory within academia, prompted by the realization that faculty turnover at his college has quietly dissolved his own generational cohort of colleagues. He traces how the profession's relationship to age and tenure has shifted since mandatory retirement at seventy was outlawed in 1993, noting that the feared 'gerontocracy' among senior faculty never materialized -- instead, the rise of adjunct labor created a different and more consequential imbalance between the haves and have-nots of academic employment. Imber contrasts the collegial, civil disagreement he witnessed among senior faculty when he arrived at Wellesley with what he calls a newer 'therapeutic censoriousness,' in which feeling has become detached from intellect well before the more recent vocabulary of cancel culture and self-censorship existed to describe it. His most striking observation is structural rather than nostalgic: institutions are built to survive the loss of any single person, a truth a senior colleague once delivered to him as plain fact rather than insult, and one he now experiences from the other side as his own 'gossip cohort' and generational touchstones disappear. The essay closes not with a resolution to retire but with a modest claim to purpose -- upholding Edward Shils's vision that higher education works best across multiple generations of teachers -- set against a closing passage from G. M. Trevelyan on the ultimately universal vanishing of every generation into the next.
points: Imber's most transferable insight for institutional leaders is structural, not sentimental: 'the truth of the essential strength of institutions is that their vitality depends on many individuals but none in particular' -- a fact that can register as either reassuring or unsettling depending on one's position in the institution.

He offers a specific historical fact useful for framing generational-turnover debates in any profession: mandatory retirement at seventy for faculty was only outlawed effective January 1, 1993, meaning the entire premise of open-ended academic careers is younger than most people assume.

His diagnosis that the feared 1990s 'gerontocracy' never emerged, but was replaced by a starker have/have-not divide between tenured and adjunct faculty, redirects a common generational-conflict narrative toward a labor-structure explanation instead.

He locates 'therapeutic censoriousness' -- the separation of feeling from intellect -- as predating and distinct from cancel culture and self-censorship debates, offering a genealogical distinction other writers on academic culture could use.
quotes: So what about the hangers-on in my own line of work? Are we threatening to turn the groves of academe into the graves of academe?

During the 1990s, a mild panic set in among administrators who feared that a gerontocracy would emerge, upsetting the balance between younger and older members of the academy. Nothing quite like that has happened. Instead, the significant growth of adjunct faculty has created a different kind of imbalance, between the haves and the have-nots.

Long before cancel culture, a kind of therapeutic censoriousness arose that mimicked the larger cultural ethos in which feeling was so drastically separated from intellect that the latter became a liability and remains so right up to our present moment.
Perhaps I am the victim of what could be called institutional dementia, seeing how the same problems recur in the often-complete absence of institutional memory.
As a senior colleague remarked to me when I left my first full-time job for another school: "You will be missed, but the institution will survive." No insult was intended.
The truth of the essential strength of institutions is that their vitality depends on many individuals but none in particular.

The sociologist Edward Shils once remarked that the promise of a truly higher education operates best with multiple generations of teachers who can enact their particular experiences of time and place.
